report:
**Short answer: No — the best current evidence does not support ginkgo biloba as an effective treatment for tinnitus.**

The Cochrane systematic review, the gold-standard source for this question, concluded that only a few good-quality randomized trials exist and that evidence is insufficient to recommend ginkgo biloba for tinnitus (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003852_ginkgo-biloba-tinnitus). This aligns with a rigorous randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial and accompanying meta-analysis of prior randomized trials, which explicitly concluded that "Ginkgo biloba does not benefit patients with tinnitus" (https://www.tinnitusjournal.com/articles/ginkgo-biloba-in-the-treatment-of-tinnitus-an-updated-literature-review.html).

A separate systematic review (Hilton and Stewart, discussed in a PMC article) similarly found no consistent benefit across the trials it examined, reinforcing that most rigorously designed studies fail to show ginkgo outperforming placebo (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3157487/).

Some studies do report positive findings—for example, trials comparing the specific standardized extract EGb 761® to pentoxifylline found "similarly effective" reductions in tinnitus loudness and annoyance—but these were not placebo-controlled comparisons, making it unclear whether either drug outperforms no treatment at all (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29855986/). Other proponents (e.g., Dovepress systematic review) argue EGb 761® specifically is "evidence-based," but this conclusion relies heavily on industry-associated trials and has been criticized for methodological inconsistency and formulation differences across ginkgo products (varying extraction standards, dosing, and trial quality).

**Conclusion:** Given the weight of independent, placebo-controlled evidence and the authoritative Cochrane assessment, the preponderance of high-quality evidence indicates ginkgo biloba does not reliably relieve tinnitus symptoms, though a specific extract (EGb 761®) has produced some positive but non-definitive results in less rigorous comparative trials.
